title: Web Systems
description: Learn GRE words through HTTP, web security, search engines, distributed data processing and fault tolerance.

cards.sentence: Tim Berners-Lee's inchoate 1989 proposal for linking documents at CERN was described by his boss as "vague but exciting".
cards.explanation: He built the first web server and browser in 1990, and the first web page went online at CERN in 1991. The three core ideas, URLs, HTTP and HTML, are still the foundation of every web system.

citations.title: A short history of the Web (CERN)

cards.sentence: A URL is analogous to a postal address: its scheme, host and path tell a client where to send a request and which resource it wants.
cards.explanation: An HTTP request names a method and a path, such as GET /index.html, and the server replies with a status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error) and a body. HTTP semantics are specified in RFC 9110.

cards.sentence: HTTP is stateless, so the connection between two requests from the same user is tenuous until a cookie carries a session identifier.
cards.explanation: Lou Montulli created cookies at Netscape in 1994. The server sets one with a Set-Cookie header and the browser returns it on later requests; attributes such as Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite limit how it can be used.

cards.sentence: A DNS lookup can follow a tortuous path: a stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, which may query a root server, a top-level-domain server and finally the domain's authoritative server.
cards.explanation: Each answer carries a time-to-live so resolvers can cache it, which keeps most lookups fast. The system is a hierarchy of delegated zones, described in RFC 1034 and 1035.

cards.sentence: In HTTP/2 over TCP, one lost packet can occlude every stream behind it, which QUIC avoids by delivering streams independently.
cards.explanation: This problem is called head-of-line blocking. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (RFC 9000, 2021), which uses UDP, builds in TLS 1.3 and lets a loss on one stream leave the others unaffected.

citations.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport (RFC 9000)

cards.definition: assert confidently or declare; as used in law, state formally as a fact
cards.sentence: A TLS certificate lets a server aver its identity: a certificate authority that browsers trust has signed a statement tying the domain name to the server's public key.
cards.explanation: The browser checks the chain up to a trusted root and then uses the key to set up an encrypted session. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, 2018) is the current version, and Let's Encrypt made free, automated certificates widespread starting in 2015-2016.

citations.title: The Transport Layer Security Protocol Version 1.3 (RFC 8446)

cards.definition: impervious; not permitting passage through its substance
cards.sentence: The same-origin policy makes the boundary between origins largely impermeable: a script from one origin cannot read responses from another unless that server opts in with CORS headers.
cards.explanation: An origin is the combination of scheme, host and port. The policy keeps a malicious page from reading, say, your logged-in email in another tab, and Access-Control-Allow-Origin lets a server deliberately relax it.

cards.definition: make impure by adding inferior or tainted substances
cards.sentence: A cross-site scripting attack can adulterate a trusted page with attacker-supplied script, which then runs with all the page's privileges.
cards.explanation: XSS comes in stored, reflected and DOM-based forms. Defenses include encoding output, a strict Content Security Policy and marking session cookies HttpOnly so scripts cannot read them.

cards.sentence: A cross-site request forgery attack can turn a logged-in browser into a dupe, sending a request the user never intended, such as a money transfer.
cards.explanation: The browser attaches cookies automatically, so the target site cannot tell the request was forged. Anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies, which Chrome began treating as Lax by default in 2020, are the main defenses.

cards.sentence: OAuth 2.0 lets a user sanction a third-party app to access an account without handing over the password.
cards.explanation: The app receives a scoped, revocable access token instead of the credentials. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top, which is how "Sign in with Google" works.

cards.sentence: Salting and deliberately slow hash functions such as bcrypt or Argon2 make offline password cracking arduous even after a database leak.
cards.explanation: A unique salt per password defeats precomputed rainbow tables, and a tunable cost factor makes each guess expensive. Argon2 won the Password Hashing Competition in 2015, and OWASP recommends it for new systems.

cards.sentence: The Heartbleed bug, inadvertently introduced into OpenSSL in 2012 and disclosed in April 2014, let attackers read up to 64 KB of a server's memory per request.
cards.explanation: A missing bounds check in the TLS heartbeat feature let a client ask for more data than it sent. The leaked memory could contain private keys and passwords, so many sites had to replace certificates and ask users to change passwords.

cards.sentence: Build tools put a content hash in static filenames, so each file is immutable and can be cached for a year; a new deploy simply produces new names.
cards.explanation: A header such as Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable tells browsers and CDNs never to revalidate. The HTML page that references the files stays short-lived, so users pick up the new names right away.

cards.sentence: A content delivery network disseminates copies of a site's files to edge servers around the world, so users fetch them from a nearby location.
cards.explanation: Akamai, founded in 1998 out of MIT research, pioneered the approach. Besides cutting latency, a CDN absorbs traffic spikes and filters some denial-of-service attacks before they reach the origin server.

cards.definition: propriety; orderliness and good taste in manners
cards.sentence: A well-behaved crawler shows decorum by fetching a site's robots.txt first and honoring its rules.
cards.explanation: The Robots Exclusion Protocol dates to 1994 and was standardized as RFC 9309 in 2022. It is a request, not access control, so sensitive content still needs authentication.

cards.sentence: Without an inverted index, answering a query would require an onerous scan of every document; the index maps each term directly to the documents that contain it.
cards.explanation: Each term has a postings list of document IDs, kept sorted so that an AND query is answered by intersecting lists. Search libraries like Lucene, which Elasticsearch builds on, store and compress these lists.

citations.title: A first take at building an inverted index (Introduction to Information Retrieval)

cards.sentence: Precision drops when many results are only tangential to the query, while recall drops when relevant documents are missing.
cards.explanation: Precision is the fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant, and recall is the fraction of relevant documents that are retrieved. For ranked lists, search teams also use measures such as nDCG that reward putting the best results first.

citations.title: Evaluation of unranked retrieval sets (Introduction to Information Retrieval)

cards.sentence: PageRank treats a link as a mark of approbation: a page matters more when important pages link to it.
cards.explanation: Larry Page and Sergey Brin described it in 1998 using a "random surfer" model with a damping factor of 0.85. The score is computed by repeatedly propagating importance along links until it stabilizes.

citations.title: The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine (Brin and Page, 1998)

cards.sentence: Search engines fight link farms and keyword stuffing, forms of chicanery meant to inflate a page's ranking.
cards.explanation: Google's Panda (2011) and Penguin (2012) updates targeted thin content and link spam, and its spam policies now list many such tactics. Ranking systems are in a permanent contest with people who try to manipulate them.

citations.title: Spam policies for Google web search

cards.definition: agent that increases the pace of a chemical action
cards.sentence: Google's 2004 MapReduce paper was a catalyst for Hadoop, which made large-scale batch processing available to anyone with a cluster.
cards.explanation: A programmer writes a map function and a reduce function, and the framework handles partitioning the data, scheduling tasks and re-running the ones that fail. Hadoop, started by Doug Cutting in 2006, was an open-source implementation.

citations.title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters (Google)

cards.sentence: In Spark, each resilient distributed dataset is derivative: it remembers the transformations that produced it, so a lost partition can be recomputed.
cards.explanation: Zaharia et al. (NSDI 2012) used this lineage instead of replicating intermediate data, which lets Spark keep working sets in memory. It is much faster than disk-based MapReduce for iterative jobs such as machine learning.

cards.sentence: A sharded database splits a large table into shards, each stored on a different server, usually by hashing a key such as the user ID.
cards.explanation: Consistent hashing (Karger et al., 1997) limits how much data must move when servers are added or removed. Hot keys and queries that join data across shards are the hard parts of this design.

cards.sentence: Under eventual consistency, replicas may be briefly discordant, but they converge once updates have propagated.
cards.explanation: Amazon's Dynamo paper (SOSP 2007) used this approach so that a shopping cart stays available even during failures. Conflicting writes are reconciled with techniques such as vector clocks or last-write-wins.

citations.title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store

cards.sentence: Brewer's contention, proved by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002, is that during a network partition a distributed system cannot be both consistent and available.
cards.explanation: Since partitions cannot be ruled out, designers choose between consistency (CP) and availability (AP) when one happens. Abadi's PACELC adds that even without a partition there is a tradeoff between latency and consistency.

citations.title: Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services (Gilbert and Lynch)

cards.sentence: Raft was designed to be more lucid than Paxos, splitting consensus into leader election, log replication and safety.
cards.explanation: Ongaro and Ousterhout presented it at USENIX ATC in 2014. Raft is used in systems such as etcd, which stores Kubernetes cluster state, and Consul.

citations.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft paper)

cards.definition: cause to be set aside; replace; make obsolete
cards.sentence: In Raft, a leader with a higher term number supersedes any older leader, so a stale leader that returns from a partition steps down.
cards.explanation: Terms act like logical clocks, and a log entry is committed only when a majority of servers have stored it. A cluster of five servers therefore keeps working with up to two failures.

cards.definition: firmly established by nature or habit
cards.sentence: At data-center scale, failures are inherent, and the Google File System paper (2003) treated component failure as the norm rather than the exception.
cards.explanation: GFS split files into large chunks, replicated each chunk (three copies by default) and used a single master to track them. Hadoop's HDFS was modeled on it.

cards.sentence: Redundancy bolsters availability: with independent replicas, a service stays up as long as at least one copy is working.
cards.explanation: "Four nines" (99.99 percent) allows about 52.6 minutes of downtime per year. Failures are often correlated, through shared power, a shared network or a bad deploy, which is why replicas in one region do not provide the full benefit.

cards.sentence: A service-level agreement may stipulate 99.9 percent monthly uptime, which allows roughly 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month.
cards.explanation: Teams usually set stricter internal service-level objectives and track an error budget, the amount of unreliability they can spend on releases. When the budget is used up, the focus shifts to stability.

cards.sentence: Exponential backoff with random jitter attenuates retry storms by spreading clients' retries out over time.
cards.explanation: Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together and create new spikes. AWS's 2015 Architecture Blog post on backoff and jitter showed that adding randomness greatly reduces total contention.

citations.title: Exponential Backoff And Jitter (AWS Architecture Blog)

cards.definition: prevent by taking action in advance
cards.sentence: A circuit breaker stops calls to a failing dependency, which helps forestall a cascading failure.
cards.explanation: It has three states: closed (normal), open (calls fail fast) and half-open (a few trial calls test recovery). Michael Nygard popularized the pattern in his 2007 book Release It!.

cards.sentence: Because PUT and DELETE are idempotent in HTTP, a retried request that arrives twice is inconsequential, whereas a repeated POST for a payment could charge a customer twice.
cards.explanation: RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE as idempotent. Payment APIs such as Stripe's accept an Idempotency-Key header so clients can retry POST requests safely.

cards.sentence: A rate limiter acts as a levee, holding back a flood of requests so that a surge, or an abusive client, cannot swamp the service.
cards.explanation: Common algorithms are the token bucket and leaky bucket. A server that limits a client replies with 429 Too Many Requests (RFC 6585), often with a Retry-After header telling the client when to try again.

cards.sentence: A few aberrant slow responses dominate when a request fans out to many servers: if each is slow 1 percent of the time, a request that touches 100 servers is slow about 63 percent of the time.
cards.explanation: The figure is 1 - 0.99^100. Dean and Barroso's "The Tail at Scale" (2013) describes remedies such as hedged requests, which send a duplicate request to a second server if the first is slow.

citations.title: The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso)

cards.sentence: Netflix's Chaos Monkey seems whimsical, randomly shutting down production instances, but it forces engineers to build services that survive failure.
cards.explanation: It was created in 2011 while Netflix moved to AWS, and it started the practice of chaos engineering: running controlled experiments to find weaknesses before real outages do.

cards.sentence: The October 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage began with a latent race condition in DynamoDB's DNS automation, which left the service's regional endpoint with an empty DNS record.
cards.explanation: A delayed component applied an old plan over a newer one, and a cleanup step then deleted the old plan, which removed every IP address for the endpoint. The event lasted about 14.5 hours, from 11:48 PM PDT on October 19 to 2:20 PM PDT on October 20, and affected EC2, load balancers, Lambda and more.

citations.title: AWS: Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption in US-EAST-1 (Oct 2025)

cards.sentence: During the same AWS event, network load balancer nodes vacillated in and out of DNS as health checks failed, until engineers disabled automatic failover.
cards.explanation: The unhealthy checks removed capacity just when it was needed. AWS turned off the automatic health-check failover at 9:36 AM PDT, which brought healthy nodes back, and re-enabled it later in the afternoon.

citations.title: AWS: Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption in US-EAST-1 (Oct 2025)

cards.sentence: On July 2, 2019, a pathological regular expression in a firewall rule caused catastrophic backtracking, driving Cloudflare's CPUs to 100 percent worldwide.
cards.explanation: The rule was deployed to the whole network at once, and the outage lasted about 27 minutes. Cloudflare's postmortem led to staged rollouts and a switch to a regex engine with guaranteed running time.

citations.title: Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019

cards.definition: narrow-mindedness; isolation; by extension, here, being cut off from one's own systems
cards.sentence: Facebook's October 2021 outage was prolonged by insularity: internal tools that depended on the same failed network made diagnosis and repair harder.
cards.explanation: A configuration change during maintenance withdrew the network routes to Facebook's DNS servers on October 4, and the services were down for about six hours. The postmortem describes how the failure also disrupted the tools engineers used to fix it.

citations.title: More details about the October 4 outage (Meta Engineering)
